entries.name: Yurt (ger)
layout: stove in the middle, flue through the crown
blueprint: legend: w felt wall, d door, s stove, . air
entries.found: in groups of 2-8 near water and pasture
entries.notes: Packed in a day: a camp may be gone when the player returns. The Mongolian word is ger ('home'); Turkic languages say yurt.

entries.name: Tipi
entries.purpose: dwelling, moved to follow the bison herds
layout: hearth in the centre, smoke exits the top
entries.found: in camps of 10-100 lodges along river valleys on the plains
entries.notes: Two ear flaps at the apex let the fire draw; the inner liner stops draughts. Women owned and raised the lodge.

entries.name: Iglu (snow house)
layout: low entrance tunnel on the lee side
entries.found: alone or in small hunting camps on sea ice and tundra in winter
entries.notes: Body heat and a lamp warm the inside to just below freezing; the blocks are sawn from a snowdrift, not packed.

entries.name: Bayt al-sha'ar (black tent)
parts: men's side and women's side divided by a curtain
layout: ridge line along the long axis
guests received at the front, family behind the curtain
entries.found: in tribal encampments of a few to a hundred tents near wells and grazing
entries.notes: Goat-hair cloth is hot in the sun and warm at night, and tightens when wet. The Arab black tent is one end of a belt of black-tent cultures reaching to the Tibetan plateau.

entries.name: Vardo
parts: shafts or hitch for one or two horses
layout: berth across the front, stove mid-ship
entries.found: on travelling routes and at fairs and race meetings across Europe
entries.notes: The Gypsy wagon: a full caravan home with carved and gilded panels. Irish Travellers used barrel-top and Reading types; both are vardos.

entries.name: Covered wagon (prairie schooner)
entries.purpose: transport and shelter for overland migrant families
layout: canvas cover as a walk-in cabin
goods and food under the bed, people on top
entries.found: in wagon trains on the emigrant trails of North America
entries.notes: Slept under the bows on the move. Every family needed one; outfitting for the Oregon Trail was the era's equivalent of buying a house.

entries.name: Aqal (aqal Soomaali)
parts: kabad woven mat walls and roof
layout: sleeping area at the back, living area near the door
thorn-bush fence ring around the camp
entries.found: in small family camps near wells and pasture across the Horn of Africa
entries.notes: Built entirely by the women of the household, dismantled and carried by camel. Colourful mats face inward.

entries.name: Chum (mya)
entries.purpose: dwelling, moved with the reindeer herds
parts: outer cover of bark or hides
layout: door facing south or away from the wind
hearth in the centre, smoke hole above
entries.found: in reindeer camps of 2-30 families across the West Siberian tundra and taiga
entries.notes: The Nenets word is mya. Cover changes with the season: white birchbark in summer, sewn reindeer hide in the -40 C winters.

entries.name: Lavvu
entries.purpose: dwelling and camp shelter, moved with the reindeer
parts: three-pole lean-together frame with no ridgepole
layout: door facing away from the prevailing wind
open fire in the middle, smoke out through the top
entries.found: in reindeer-herding camps and at modern Sámi festivals across northern Fennoscandia
entries.notes: Lighter and quicker to pitch than the goahti; the triangular frame needs no central post. Still the iconic Sámi tent.

entries.name: Yaranga
layout: wind shell open in the middle
polog sleeping tent pitched inside the shell
entries.found: in reindeer camps of the Chukotka tundra and the Koryak highlands
entries.notes: The two-skin trick: the outer yaranga breaks the wind, the inner polog is the warm, snug room. One yaranga houses a whole family.

entries.name: Goahti
layout: a low catenary dome 5 blocks across
entrance tunnel on the sheltered side
entries.found: at historic Sámi settlement sites across northern Norway, Sweden and Finland
entries.notes: Lasted about ten years before the turf grew together into a smooth green mound. Some were rebuilt so often a family simply kept one going.

entries.name: Tupiq (summer tent)
entries.found: at summer caribou and fishing camps across the Arctic
entries.notes: Men struck the poles and women sewed the skins. In summer the iglu is retired and the tupiq takes over; the pair is the core of mobile Inuit life.

entries.name: Qarmaq
parts: low semi-permanent wall of stone, sod or snow blocks
layout: a low dome or truncated cone 4 blocks across
entries.found: at seasonal camps across the Canadian Arctic and Greenland
entries.notes: A hybrid of iglu and tent for the awkward seasons: too warm for a snow house, too cold for a skin tent. Built until the 1950s.

entries.name: Sbra-nag (black tent, gur)
parts: square or rectangular woven yak-hair cover
single ridge pole on two stout posts
side guys pinned to the ground
two trapezoidal roof halves joined at the ridge
layout: central hearth under the opening between the cover halves
entries.found: on the high plateau pastures of the Tibetan Plateau, Amdo and Kham
entries.notes: The easternmost black tent. The gabled rTse-sbra variant and the white-canvas gur exist for guests and migration. Woven so loose it breathes smoke but swells shut in rain.

entries.name: Siah chador (black tent)
parts: ridge pole on two main posts
layout: ridge line along the long axis
entries.found: along the seasonal migration routes between lowland winter and highland summer pasture in Iran
entries.notes: Iran's huge transhumant population winters in the warm south and summers in the Zagros. Same tensile black-tent tech as the Arab bayt al-sha'ar.

entries.name: Ehan (Tuareg tent)
parts: interior sleeping mats and leather chests
layout: ridge line along the long axis
frontal opening facing the morning sun
entries.found: in camel-herding camps across the Sahara and Sahel, from Algeria to Mali and Niger
entries.notes: The Tuareg 'house of skins'. Women own the tents; the tent pole spacing shows the wealth of the household.

entries.name: Suudu hudo (bukkaru)
parts: domed grass roof on reed-mat walls
millet-stalk support posts in the dry season
layout: calf-tying rope in front of each hut
entries.found: in Wodaabe and Fulani cattle camps across the Sahel from Senegal to Sudan
entries.notes: Completely portable: dismantled and lashed onto a camel or donkey for each move. The Wodaabe suudu proper is often just a thorn-branch screen, open to the sky.

entries.name: Enkaji
entries.purpose: dwelling within a seasonally relocated village
layout: fireplace at the far end, sleeping shelves along the walls
entries.found: in enkang homesteads around cattle kraals across Kenya and Tanzania
entries.notes: Not carried: rebuilt from scratch at each new pasture. A woman's house, her measure of skill; the dung plaster is re-coated yearly.

entries.name: Matjieshuis (reed mat house)
entries.purpose: dwelling, moved with the herds or the game
entries.found: in seasonal camps of the Karoo and the Kalahari fringe
entries.notes: Afrikaans for 'mat house'. The Khoekhoe built them for pastoral moves; the San used similar domes of grass and brush.

entries.name: Gunyah
parts: lean-to or semi-conical frame of saplings
layout: built against a tree or on open ground
entries.found: across eastern and southeastern Aboriginal Australia
entries.notes: Bark came from eucalypts; the camp was a light seasonal affair, easy to build in an afternoon and leave behind.

entries.name: Miamia (mia mia)
layout: open side to the fire and away from wind
entries.found: in southeastern Aboriginal camps
entries.notes: The southeastern name for the same bark-shelter tech as the gunyah; catalogued separately for its distinct name and region.

entries.name: Wigwam
entries.found: in spring and summer fishing, hunting and gathering camps across the eastern woodlands
entries.notes: Not a one-piece shelter like a tipi: rebuilt at each seasonal site in the annual round. The word itself comes from Algonquian 'wikewam', 'house'.

entries.name: Wickiup
layout: fire in the centre with a smoke hole above
entries.found: in small family camps across the Great Basin and the Southwest
entries.notes: The Apache wickiup could be raised in an hour and was the lightest serious shelter in the Southwest. Same family of domed brush huts as the African bukkaru.

entries.name: Hogan
layout: hearth in the centre, smoke hole above
entries.found: in Navajo homesteads across the Four Corners; now mostly ceremonial
entries.notes: More permanent than a wickiup but of the same migratory pastoral culture; abandoned and rebuilt as the family moved. The old conical form came first, the eight-sided one later.

entries.name: Coliba (coliba ciobănească)
layout: near the fold on the high pasture
entries.found: on the Carpathian summer pastures during the transhumance
entries.notes: Romanian shepherds drove their flocks to the high meadows every summer; the coliba is where the cheese happened. Related to the Albanian and Bulgarian koliba.

entries.name: Toldo
entries.purpose: dwelling, moved with the horse herds
parts: hide cover leaning against the wind
open side facing away from the wind
layout: fire in front of the opening
entries.found: on the Patagonian steppe and the Pampas
entries.notes: A hide windbreak more than a tent; the Tehuelche mastered horse nomadism on these. The Mapuche adopted and spread it on the horse frontier.

entries.name: Shabono
parts: one continuous palm-thatch roof over the ring
layout: family hearths spaced around the inside of the ring
open plaza in the middle for feasts and duels
entries.found: one per Yanomami village of 50-400 people in the Amazon rainforest of Brazil and Venezuela
entries.notes: Semi-permanent: occupied for a few years, then the whole shabono is burned or abandoned. The largest single-roofed dwelling in this catalogue by far.

entries.name: Urasa (uraha)
parts: central fire pit with hanging kettle
layout: pillars in a ring, poles leaning on the ring
fire in the centre under the smoke hole
entries.found: at summer pasture camps and yhyakh festival sites in Yakutia
entries.notes: The monumental Mogol urasa of a clan chief reached 10-12 m and held some 100 people. Ordinary summer urasas were 5-7 m across and soon overtaken by log balaans for winter.

entries.name: Rebo
entries.purpose: dwelling, moved with the pashmina herds
parts: low wall of stones or dung against the wind
open smoke slot along the roof
layout: a hexagonal plan about 6 by 5 blocks
low walls, open top for smoke
stove in the middle, drying yak cheese on the roof
entries.found: in Changthang plateau camps above 4,000 m, Leh district of Ladakh
entries.notes: Pashmina goat herders live whole lives in rebos at -35 C. Canvas and parachute rebos now outnumber yak hair, a sign the craft is dying.

entries.name: Khaïma (Atlas tent)
parts: ridge pole on two main posts
dark wool canopy of sewn strips
layout: ridge line along the long axis
entries.found: on the seasonal pastures of the Middle and High Atlas
entries.notes: The Maghrebi link in the black-tent belt from Arabia to Tibet. Wool, not hair, and usually dark brown rather than black.

entries.name: Kibitka
entries.purpose: covered wagon and, for Kalmyks, felt yurt
parts: arched bows over a wagon or sleigh
cloth or felt stretched over the bows
steppe yurt variant with felt walls
layout: a wagon with an arched roof
also the Kalmyk felt yurt for tax purposes
entries.found: on the Russian imperial steppe, Volga to the Altai
entries.notes: One word, two things: the Russian covered cart (and the exile's transport) and the Kalmyk felt tent. The 'kibitka tax' was levied on every nomadic dwelling.

entries.name: Ger on a cart (ger tergen)
entries.purpose: elite dwelling and mobile throne room
parts: a yurt fixed permanently to a huge four-wheeled cart
layout: a yurt on a wagon chassis
the Khan travels inside his own house
the camp forms a wall of carts around the ger
entries.found: in the royal camps of the Mongol Empire, described by William of Rubruck in 1254
entries.notes: William of Rubruck saw wagoned ger with axles 'as large as ships' masts'. Reserved for the elite; ordinary families struck the yurt for every move.

entries.name: Scythian wagon-house
entries.purpose: wagon-borne dwelling of the steppe aristocracy
parts: felt-walled cabin or yurt on the chassis
layout: a wagon large enough to live in
the ruling elite travelled in felt-covered wagons while the poor herded on foot
entries.found: along the migration routes of the western Eurasian steppe, modern Ukraine and southern Russia
entries.notes: Herodotus (Histories 4.46) records the Scythians living in wagons; Greeks called them amaxobii, 'the wagon-dwellers'. Dimensions not documented.

entries.name: Travel trailer (caravan)
parts: boxed shell on a single axle
layout: bed at the front, dinette mid-ship, kitchen at the door
entries.found: at campgrounds, festivals and full-time on the road across Europe and North America
entries.notes: The modern heir of the vardo: Gordon-Cumming's first caravan was built in 1884. Today a serious full-time dwelling for a mobile population.

entries.name: Camper van
parts: interior berth, tiny kitchen, swivel seats
layout: small kitchen unit along one wall
entries.found: anywhere with a road; huge in Australia, New Zealand and Europe
entries.notes: The self-drive end of the nomadic spectrum: no hitch needed, sleeper and transport in one. The VW Type 2 made it a way of life in the 1960s.
